q: Hypertensive emergency in this recap. Systolic is typically above what, with end-organ signs?

opts.why: Hypertensive emergency is typically a systolic over 180 with end-organ signs (headache, bounding pulse, ringing ears, nosebleed, nausea, dizziness, altered).
90 to 120 is a normal systolic in this recap, not the emergency cut.
90 is the low end of normal systolic here, not the hypertensive-emergency number.
Some texts call 130 the top of normal. Emergency here is over 180 with signs.

q: High blood pressure only. Nitroglycerin in this recap?

opts.t: Do not give it just for BP
opts.why: Do not give nitroglycerin solely to treat hypertension. It drops, then rebounds, and the rebound is when rupture risk is highest.

opts.t: Give it for a nosebleed too
opts.why: A nosebleed is an end-organ sign of high pressure. It is not a reason to give nitro for the pressure.
Rebound is the danger. Do not chase it with more nitro for pressure alone.

opts.t: Hold it only if they hurt
opts.why: Chest-pain nitro is a different protocol question. Pressure-only is a no.

q: Classic aortic dissection pain in this recap?

opts.why: Sudden, 10 out of 10 from the start, tearing chest pain radiating to the back between the shoulder blades.
Crushing, squeezing pressure that builds is the MI wording in this recap, not dissection.

opts.t: Slow mild ache in the chest
opts.why: Dissection is maximal at onset, not a slow mild ache.
Classic radiation in this recap is to the back between the shoulder blades, not down the arm.

q: An implanted defibrillator fires. Can you touch them in this recap?

opts.why: ICD electricity is low and internal. You may feel a tiny jolt at most. Safe to touch when it fires.

opts.t: No, clear them like an AED
opts.why: Clearing is for an AED or a vest. An ICD shock is internal and low.
Hands off is the vest and AED rule. An ICD shock is safe to touch.

opts.t: Only if they still have pulse
opts.why: Touch is safe either way. Arrest still gets standard CPR and AED.

q: External defibrillator vest is counting down. What does this recap want?

opts.why: The vest warns out loud, then delivers a high-energy external shock. Do not touch while it is shocking, like an AED.
Holding through the shock is not the vest rule. Hands off like an AED.
ICD touch is safe because that shock is internal. The vest is an external shock. Hands off.
The vest talks. Follow the voice. Then standard resuscitation as needed.

q: VAD patient, no pulse, talking. What does this recap say?

opts.why: Many VADs are continuous flow, so there is no palpable pulse. If they are conscious and talking, they are perfusing.
Do not start CPR just because there is no pulse. Talking means they are perfusing.

opts.t: No pulse means they are dead
opts.why: No pulse is expected on many continuous-flow VADs. Talking is the perfusion check.

opts.t: No pulse means the VAD failed
opts.why: A missing pulse on a talking VAD patient is expected with continuous flow, not proof the pump failed.

q: Unconscious VAD patient. Who does this recap want you to call?

opts.why: Find and call the phone number on the controller. The VAD team talks you through CPR, troubleshooting, and destination.
The extra step is the VAD team number on the controller, not a guess at the closest hospital.
This recap wants the number on the controller so the VAD team can talk you through it.
Do not wait on family. Call the number on the controller.

q: AED says no shock advised. What does this recap want next?

opts.why: No shock advised only means it is not VF or pulseless VT. Check a pulse. No pulse: keep CPR. Pulse: ROSC.
You still check a pulse after no-shock-advised. Then CPR or ROSC.
No shock only means not VF or pulseless VT. It can be asystole or PEA. Check a pulse.
No shock is not proof of a pulse. You still check.

q: Pediatric arrest in this recap. What is the usual path?

opts.why: Kids usually do not arrest from primary VF. Respiratory failure, hypoxia, bradycardia, then PEA or asystole. Still use the AED. Expect no shock more often.
Primary VF is the adult pattern. Kids usually start with a breathing problem.
PEA is later in the kid path, after hypoxia and a slow heart, not first.
Asystole is later in the kid path. The usual start is respiratory failure and hypoxia.

q: AED says check pads on a hairy chest. What does this recap want?

opts.t: Shave or rip the first pads
opts.why: Shave with the included razor, or stick one pad set on and rip it off to wax hair, then apply a second set.

opts.t: Skip the AED for the hair
opts.why: Do not skip the AED. Get the pads to stick.
The AED may say push firmly. The fix in this recap is still shave or wax, then a second set.
Fix the pads now. The AED will keep saying check pads until they stick.

q: AED shock during transport in this recap?

opts.why: Stop the vehicle briefly for defibrillation. Movement affects analysis and safety.
Do not shock while rolling. Stop first.
This recap wants you to stop for the shock.
Do not wait until the hospital. Stop briefly and shock now.

q: Pacemaker fails in this recap. What can you do in the field?

opts.why: The heart reverts to the old slow rhythm. Treat bradycardia and shock. Rapid transport. You cannot fix the pacemaker.
You cannot fix the pacemaker in the field.

opts.t: Wait it out on scene now
opts.why: Do not wait. Treat the slow rate and shock, then rapid transport.
Treat the slow-perfusion problem. Pads go on, not directly over the device.
